title: Sycamore Tree Tips Chemicals in Iran Jam
description:
Middle East shipping disruptions are boosting US companies bruised by cheap Chinese supply, according to Sycamore Tree Capital Partners. “It really slows down the ability for some of those Asian-based chemical companies to produce,” Trey Parker, the asset manager’s co-founder and chief investment officer, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s Phil Brendel in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “You’re going to have more US- and European-based chemical companies have an inherent advantage,” Parker added. They also discuss health-care relative value, the outlook for debt defaults, a slowdown in liability management exercises and opportunity in credit secondaries.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
one_line_summary: Trey Parker, CIO of Sycamore Tree Capital Partners, discusses the current state of credit markets, the opportunities in credit secondaries, and the impact of AI on software companies.
summary: The discussion highlights the importance of good old-fashioned credit selection, focusing on companies with real staying power and moats that are difficult to transition out of. Trey also notes that when software companies do get distressed, it's not just a capital structure issue, and that customers will have greater concerns, making the potential deterioration of those companies more dire and more risky for investors.
market_signals: The credit secondary market did $20 billion of volume last year and is expected to move higher over the next several years.
Discounts upwards of 20 to 25 percent to NAVs can materialize in the credit secondary market.
The most distressed sector is now technology, with software companies being unique animals with high leverage and concerns about AI disruption.
There is $40 billion plus of stressed or distressed software loans in the market, but the fundamentals are not yet proving that out.
Net and gross retention rates within the software space are at relatively healthy levels.
framework_insights: The importance of understanding the complexities of credit across multiple cycles and having a team with experience navigating different economic and credit cycles.
The need for good old-fashioned credit selection, focusing on companies with real staying power and moats that are difficult to transition out of.
The impact of AI on software companies will be a function of how easily replaceable or sort of how easy particular software is to transition out of.
The importance of focusing on pricing models that are more usage-based or subscription-based, where the utilization isn't just a headcount and employee-based driven factor.
The need to be careful about betting on good company, bad balance sheet, as the moats for companies are shrinking and the risk of obsolescence is evolving much more quickly.
market_relevance: The conversation highlights the current state of credit markets and the opportunities in credit secondaries, which is relevant for investors looking to navigate the complex credit landscape. The discussion also touches on the impact of AI on software companies, which is a key theme for investors to consider in the technology sector.

title: Davidson Kempner Sees a $770 Billion Stressed Debt Opportunity
description:
US companies with $770 billion in loans are hitting a wall as interest rates stay elevated, according to Davidson Kempner. “We’re in year three of what’s already the longest default cycle in 20 years,” Suzy Gibbons, the hedge fund’s head of research, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s David Havens in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “About a third of the market is stressed based on fundamental credit data,” she said. They also discuss liability management exercises, software defaults, distressed-debt returns and the broader impact of leveraged-debt stress on markets.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
one_line_summary: Davidson Kempner's research highlights a $770 billion stressed debt opportunity in the US leverage loan and direct lending markets, driven by high leverage and weak credit fundamentals.
summary: The Credit Edge podcast features Susie Gibbons, partner and head of research at Davidson Kempner, discussing the firm's research on stressed debt in the US leverage loan and direct lending markets. Gibbons notes that the problems in these markets are broader than just the software sector and have been building over time, with a third of the market considered stressed based on fundamental credit metrics such as leverage over 7 times and interest coverage ratios below 1.5 times. The research suggests that the issues in these markets are not yet fully reflected in market prices, with many loans still trading near par despite underlying credit weaknesses.
key_themes: Stressed debt in US leverage loan and direct lending markets
High leverage and weak credit fundamentals
market_signals: A third of the US leverage loan and direct lending markets are considered stressed, representing a $770 billion opportunity
Leverage in these markets is higher than appreciated, with reported EBITDA leverage over 7 times and interest coverage ratios below 1.5 times
The market is not yet fully reflecting the underlying credit weaknesses, with many loans still trading near par
The direct lending market is opaque, making it difficult to determine the true value of loans
The leverage loan market prices risk, but there may be a tolerance for high leverage in certain sectors
framework_insights: The current credit cycle is fundamentally different from prior cycles due to higher starting leverage and valuations
The use of adjusted EBITDA can mask true leverage in these markets, with add-backs increasing over time
Liability management exercises can delay but not solve underlying credit problems, with many companies becoming repeat defaulters
The flood of capital into private equity and leverage credit has led to loosening of underwriting standards
Opportunistic credit investors can capitalize on stressed debt opportunities by purchasing loans at a discount
market_relevance: The research highlights the potential for significant losses in the US leverage loan and direct lending markets, which could have broader implications for credit markets and investors. Opportunistic credit investors may be able to capitalize on stressed debt opportunities, but the market's failure to fully reflect underlying credit weaknesses poses a risk to investors who are not adequately prepared.

title: BDC Bond Bust Creates Opportunity for $622 Billion Asset Manager MFS
description:
A retail exodus from business-development companies has dragged their debt to levels that are starting to look attractive, according to MFS Investment Management. “Pressure for redemptions that they’re facing likely ends up creating some opportunities within the public credit markets,” Alex Mackey, the firm’s co-chief investment officer for fixed income, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s Robert Schiffman in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “You can line up all the public and the private BDCs and you can go through and see which ones have the leverage metrics that are most attractive,” said Mackey, whose firm oversees $622 billion in assets. They also discuss the deluge of technology sector debt issuance and how wide credit spreads would have to go before they’d look attractive.

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
one_line_summary: MFS Investment Management's CIO of Fixed Income, Alex Mackie, discusses the current market environment, positioning for potential risks, and opportunities in the credit market.
summary: The conversation covers the current state of the credit market, with spreads at long-term averages, and the potential risks of a recession, inflation, and geopolitical events. Alex Mackie mentions that MFS is not highly convicted of a step function change in the market but is prepared for potential risks. The discussion also touches on the impact of AI on various sectors and the opportunities it presents for credit investors. The CIO emphasizes the importance of being patient and waiting for better value propositions in the market.
market_signals: High yield spreads have widened out but come back down to around long-term averages
IG spreads are also around long-term averages
Yields have moved higher, improving the value proposition of fixed income
Demand for fixed income continues to be healthy, with bond offerings being well oversubscribed
MFS is looking for spreads to increase to around 120 basis points, a long-term average, before getting excited about deploying more capital
framework_insights: The importance of considering both macro and micro perspectives when evaluating the market
The need to be prepared for potential risks, such as recession and inflation, and to have a plan in place to take advantage of market opportunities
The impact of AI on various sectors and the potential opportunities it presents for credit investors
The importance of being patient and waiting for better value propositions in the market
The use of long-term averages and medians as a starting point for evaluating market valuations
market_relevance: The discussion provides insights into the current market environment and the potential risks and opportunities in the credit market, which is relevant for investors looking to navigate the current landscape.

title: PGIM Sees 'Chilling Effect' on Private Credit From BDC Storm
description:
Business development company turmoil is making direct lenders cautious on corporate debt risk, according to PGIM, which oversees more than $200 billion in private credit. “It’ll have a bit of a chilling effect,” Matt Harvey, the firm’s global head of middle-market direct lending, tells Bloomberg News’ James Crombie and Bloomberg Intelligence’s Matthew Geudtner in the latest Credit Edge podcast. “As a lender you’re a little bit more conservative, you’re a little bit more rational in terms of your view on how to structure the asset, how to price it,” Harvey says. They also discuss default rates, loan marks, the consumer staples sector and relative value in European direct lending.

 

See omnystudio.com/listener for privacy information.
one_line_summary: PGIM's global head of middle market direct lending discusses the evolution of private credit, its current state, and the value proposition it offers to borrowers and investors.
summary: Private credit has grown significantly over the years, with direct lending becoming a substantial part of it. The middle market lending landscape has evolved, with Chicago being a key hub. PGIM oversees more than $200 million in private credit and focuses on providing longer-term capital to fund events such as acquisitions, recapitalizations, and major growth financing. The company's direct lending strategy involves leverage loans privately negotiated for companies, with a focus on the middle market. The scale of businesses being prospected, selected, and lent to has expanded, with the traditional definition of middle market being $25-75 million of EBITDA.
market_signals: The high-yield index yield is around 7.5%, with a credit quality of B1 and maturities just under 5 years.
The leverage loan index yield is around 8.5%, with a credit quality of B1/B2.
The illiquidity premium for direct lending can be around 100 basis points above comparable liquid loans.
The average credit quality in the direct lending loan world is in the B1 to B3 range.
framework_insights: The definition of private credit has broadened over time to include more than just direct lending, such as stress debt, special finance, real estate, infrastructure lending, and mezzanine.
The value proposition of private credit lies in its ability to provide longer-term capital, higher execution certainty, and more flexibility than traditional bank loans.
The key to delivering excess return in private credit is to identify and underwrite risks, structure the loan package to address those risks, and price them appropriately.
The illiquidity premium in private credit can be a significant source of excess return for investors.
market_relevance: The growth of private credit and direct lending has significant implications for investors and markets, as it provides an alternative source of funding for companies and offers a unique value proposition for investors seeking yield and diversification.
